analysis.one_liner: Lets workers and consumers sue in court over race discrimination despite signed arbitration agreements.
analysis.headline: The bill was introduced on November 20, 2025 and sent to the House Judiciary Committee, where no action has been taken since; it has 21 Democratic cosponsors and no Republicans.
analysis.plain_summary: Employers and many companies require workers and customers to sign agreements before a dispute happens, forcing them to settle any claim in private arbitration instead of court, and often barring them from joining class actions. This bill would let a person alleging race, color, or national-origin discrimination or harassment choose to go to court instead, voiding those pre-signed arbitration clauses and class-action waivers for such cases. It covers only race discrimination, not other kinds.
analysis.who_benefits: Workers, tenants, customers, and other ordinary people who face race discrimination or harassment by an employer or company that required them to sign an arbitration agreement — they could take their case to a public court, where proceedings are on the record and precedents can protect others, and could join class or collective actions.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People facing race discrimination under arbitration clauses

how_it_helps.text: At the claimant's election, a pre-dispute arbitration agreement or pre-dispute class-action waiver would have no validity or force in a case alleging discrimination, harassment, or retaliation based on race, color, or national origin under federal, Tribal, state, or local law.
A court, not an arbitrator, would decide whether the law applies, even if the contract tries to hand that question to the arbitrator.
A person could also act as a named representative of a class or collective action, restoring group lawsuits that arbitration clauses typically block.
The change applies to disputes that arise after enactment, so it would cover future claims rather than reopening past ones.

analysis.who_pays: Employers and businesses that use mandatory arbitration clauses would lose a shield: discrimination cases could end up in public court, with jury trials, discovery, higher defense costs, and class actions, and any private agreements signed after the bill becomes law could not lock those claims into arbitration.

drawbacks.text: It covers only race, color, and national-origin discrimination. Forced arbitration for other claims — sex discrimination beyond what a 2022 law covers, wage theft, consumer disputes — remains enforceable, so the underlying problem persists for many workers.

Employers argue that arbitration resolves disputes faster and cheaper than court and that ending mandatory arbitration raises litigation costs for businesses, costs that critics say can be passed to workers and consumers; the bill also limits what parties can agree to by contract in advance.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For a person with a real discrimination claim, the gain is concrete: a public forum instead of a private arbitrator paid through the company's program, plus the ability to join with others in a class action. The main cost falls on employers facing more litigation, and the bill is deliberately narrow, leaving forced arbitration in place for every other kind of dispute.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in the House and referred to the Judiciary Committee, which has not taken it up, so it sits with no hearing, no vote, and no Senate companion movement.

narrative.text: Representative Wesley Bell introduced the bill in the House on November 20, 2025.
The same day, it was referred to the House Committee on the Judiciary, and no further action — no hearing, markup, or floor vote — appears in the record since then.
It has 21 cosponsors, all Democrats; no Republican has signed on.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Employers and companies that rely on mandatory arbitration clauses are better off so far, because the bill has not advanced and their agreements remain enforceable for race-discrimination claims.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: So far, employers that use arbitration clauses

for.name: Rep. Wesley Bell
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to the House Judiciary Committee.

for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill; no House Republican cosponsored it.

against.role: Chair of the committee of referral
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup in the months since the bill was referred, leaving it without a path to the floor.

sides.party_line_note: All 21 cosponsors are Democrats; no Republican has signed on, and the bill has had no vote where party counts would show.

industries.industry: Employers and businesses that require arbitration agreements
industries.note: The bill strips the enforceability of pre-signed arbitration clauses and class-action waivers in race-discrimination cases, exposing those firms to public-court litigation and class actions they currently avoid.
Race-discrimination claims could exit the private arbitration system at the claimant's election, reducing a category of paid arbitrations and shifting them to the courts.

analysis.trajectory: A bill introduced late in the first session with 21 Democratic cosponsors, no Republican support, and no committee action typically dies in committee unless leadership intervenes; absent a markup or floor schedule, it is unlikely to advance before the Congress ends.
